Median Triangle

GeometryTrianglesArea
Game: Move the three corners of a triangle and watch the blue triangle built from its three medians.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and press the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to name the points or to light up the half-sides.
Look for the math

A median joins a corner of a triangle to the middle of the opposite side. The three medians do not form a triangle where they are drawn, but lay their lengths end to end and they do. The blue triangle is made that way. Drag any corner: its share of the whole triangle never moves.

What the old applet draws

The dots M_a, M_b, M_c sit at the middles of BC, CA, AB. The red lines AM_a, BM_b, CM_c are the medians. The three pink corner pieces and the pink triangle E M_a F are four copies of the medial triangle, each with a quarter of the area. The blue triangle B M_b E has sides m_b, m_a, m_c: exactly the three medians. Tick "hint" to see that each midpoint divides its side into two equal halves.

The small triangle in the article

Let G be the centroid, where the medians meet. It lies two thirds of the way from a vertex to the opposite midpoint. Reflect G in M_a to get the article's point D. Then BG = 2m_b/3, GD = 2m_a/3 and BD = 2m_c/3: the sides of triangle BDG are two thirds of the medians. The medians cut ABC into six triangles of equal area, so BGM_a has 1/6 of it. Since M_a is the midpoint of GD, triangle BDG has twice that area: 2/6 = 1/3 of ABC.

Scale by three halves

The blue triangle has the same shape as BDG, with every side 3/2 times as long. Areas scale by the square of the side ratio:

area(median triangle) = (3/2)2 × (1/3) × area(ABC) = (3/4) × area(ABC).

One small difference between sources: the Java applet's own D is the reflection of A in M_a, the fourth corner of a parallelogram, while the article's D above is the reflection of G. Both appear in the two pictures; only the article's BDG has the two-thirds sides.

What was checked

The logic test tries eight hand-picked shapes and 600 random triangles. In all of them the blue area is 3/4 of ABC, BDG has two-third median sides and 1/3 of the area, and Heron's formula on the three medians gives the same blue area. Every constructed point is also compared with a second transcription of the applet's Compute() and init() bytecode. The source page still states the claim, but the live cut-the-knot page now shows a GeoGebra picture instead of the Java applet; a 2014 Wayback capture of that same address embeds APPLET CODE="MedianTriangle" with the "Show names" and "hint" checkboxes.

Drag C almost onto the line AB. The triangle flattens and both areas shrink together, but the blue triangle still takes exactly three quarters.
